working-safely-in-the-workshop.heading: Before work begins
working-safely-in-the-workshop.body: A timber workshop is a shared work area, so safe conduct matters from the moment you enter. Wear covered shoes that protect your feet from dropped tools, timber and off-cuts. Tie back long hair so it cannot fall forward or become caught. Approved eye protection must be worn during work where dust, chips or small particles may be produced. Move calmly and stay aware of the people around you. Running, pushing, throwing objects or fooling around can quickly cause an injury.

working-safely-in-the-workshop.heading: Using tools and machines
working-safely-in-the-workshop.body: Only use a machine after the teacher has given you permission. Permission applies to the person and the task at that time; it is not general approval to use the machine later. Follow marked safety zones. Only one person may be inside a machine safety zone while the machine is being used. Use tools only for their intended purpose and handle them with care. When you finish, return each tool to its correct storage place.

working-safely-in-the-workshop.heading: Keeping the area safe
working-safely-in-the-workshop.body: A clear workspace reduces trips, cuts and confusion. Place useful materials neatly and remove off-cuts from benches, floors and walkways as work continues. Do not leave tools, timber or waste where someone could step on them or knock them over. If you are unsure about a tool, machine, safety rule or what to do next, stop work and ask. Guessing is not worth the risk.

timber-words-and-properties.heading: Hardwood and softwood
timber-words-and-properties.body: Hardwood and softwood describe the type of tree timber comes from rather than how hard it feels. Hardwoods come from broadleaf trees, while softwoods come from conifer trees that usually have needles and cones. Different timber species have different strengths, colours, textures and patterns.

timber-words-and-properties.heading: Grain, density and knots
timber-words-and-properties.body: Grain is the direction and pattern of wood fibres. Straight grain often has an even appearance. Tight grain has growth rings close together, while loose grain has rings spaced further apart. Density describes how much wood is packed into a space, so denser timber usually feels heavier than less dense timber of the same size. A knot forms where a branch once grew and can change the strength, texture and appearance of timber.

timber-words-and-properties.heading: Weather resistance and workability
timber-words-and-properties.body: Weather resistance is a timber’s ability to cope with moisture, sunlight and changing outdoor conditions. Workability describes how easily timber can be sawn, drilled, shaped, sanded and finished while producing a neat result. These words help you compare material characteristics instead of choosing only by appearance.

manufactured-wood-products.heading: From timber to engineered products
manufactured-wood-products.body: Manufactured wood products combine smaller pieces of wood with adhesives, heat or pressure. Manufacturers may use thin veneers, long strands, fibres or small particles. This can produce sheets, beams or panels with predictable shapes and properties. The size, direction and arrangement of the wood pieces affects the final product.

manufactured-wood-products.heading: Common structures
manufactured-wood-products.body: Plywood is built from thin veneers glued in layers with changing grain directions. OSB uses long wood strands arranged in planned directions and pressed into large sheets. LVL is made from veneers bonded with most grain running in the same direction. CLT uses layers of solid boards placed at right angles. Fibreboard and particleboard use smaller wood pieces, while wood-plastic composite combines wood fibres or particles with plastic.

manufactured-wood-products.heading: Looking beyond the label
manufactured-wood-products.body: A manufactured product is not automatically environmentally better just because it uses small logs, off-cuts or recycled material. Consider where the wood came from, the manufacture process, transport, product life, repair options and what happens at the end of use. Check claims carefully rather than relying on a single label.

reading-the-original-footstool-plan.heading: Start with the title
reading-the-original-footstool-plan.body: The original Footstool plan is presented across two pages. Read the title and labels carefully. Technical drawings show the same object from several directions. A front view, side view or top view shows the shape as if you were looking directly at that face. Each view gives different information, so read them together.

reading-the-original-footstool-plan.heading: Read dimensions and symbols
reading-the-original-footstool-plan.body: Dimensions are written measurements that show the intended size or location of features. Dimension lines, extension lines and arrowheads connect each written measurement to the feature it describes. The diameter symbol, Ø, means the following dimension refers to the full width of a circular object or hole through its centre. The plan uses a scale of 1:2, meaning the drawing is at half the intended full size.

reading-the-original-footstool-plan.heading: Trust the written information
reading-the-original-footstool-plan.body: Written dimensions on the original two-page plan are more reliable than measuring a screen preview. A preview may be enlarged, reduced, cropped or stretched to fit a device. Compare the views and follow dimension lines carefully. If a label, line, symbol or view is unclear, pause and ask before continuing.

third-angle-and-isometric-communication.heading: Related views
third-angle-and-isometric-communication.body: Third-angle projection uses separate but related views of the same object. The front elevation shows the object from the front, the plan shows it from above and the right-hand elevation shows its right side. Each view shows two dimensions at a time and avoids the distortion of perspective.

third-angle-and-isometric-communication.heading: Matching features
third-angle-and-isometric-communication.body: A line, edge, hole or surface shown in one view may appear differently in another. A feature that looks like a rectangle in the front elevation might appear as a narrow edge in the plan. Compare position, alignment and shape across the related views. Hidden details may be shown with dashed lines when a feature cannot be seen from that direction.

third-angle-and-isometric-communication.heading: Isometric communication
third-angle-and-isometric-communication.body: An isometric drawing shows three sides at once, so it looks three-dimensional and helps a reader picture the overall form. It does not replace the plan, front elevation and right-hand elevation when precise information is required. Orthogonal views communicate accurate relationships; isometric drawing helps communicate the whole object.

developing-a-personal-emblem.heading: Researching meaningful ideas
developing-a-personal-emblem.body: A personal emblem is a small visual design that represents something about you. It might show an interest, value, place, activity, animal, object or idea. Look at how designers simplify real objects into clear shapes and use line, balance and negative space. Avoid copying an existing design; collect ideas that can be combined or changed into an original result.

developing-a-personal-emblem.heading: Creating three concepts
developing-a-personal-emblem.body: Develop three distinct thumbnail concepts before choosing a final direction. A thumbnail is a small, quick sketch used to test an idea. Vary the main symbol, layout, border shape, viewpoint or arrangement. Keep outlines simple and easy to recognise. Fine textures, crowded patterns and tiny features can become unclear when a design is reduced in size.

developing-a-personal-emblem.heading: Choosing and refining
developing-a-personal-emblem.body: Compare the three concepts using clear criteria: personal meaning, originality, balance, simplicity, readability and use of space. Redraw the chosen concept carefully and check proportions, spacing and line quality. Use feedback to revise unclear shapes, remove unnecessary detail or strengthen the main idea.

functional-design-and-evaluation.heading: Designing for a purpose
functional-design-and-evaluation.body: Every product is created to do a job. This job is called its function. A good design begins by thinking about the person who will use the product and what they need it to do. A successful design is practical, comfortable to use and suitable for its intended purpose.

functional-design-and-evaluation.heading: Looking at quality
functional-design-and-evaluation.body: Quality means more than a product looking neat. A quality product should suit its purpose, feel stable during normal use and show careful workmanship. Straight edges, smooth surfaces, accurate measurements and well-finished details all contribute to the overall quality. Careful observation provides useful evidence instead of relying on personal opinion alone.

functional-design-and-evaluation.heading: Evaluating and improving
functional-design-and-evaluation.body: Evaluation judges how well a design meets its intended function. The strongest evaluations are based on observations, measurements or other reliable information rather than guesses. Comparing the finished product with the original design goals helps identify what worked well and what could be improved. Name one realistic improvement and explain the difference it would make.

aesthetic-design-and-evaluation.heading: What aesthetics means
aesthetic-design-and-evaluation.body: Aesthetics describes how a designed object looks and feels to a viewer. It includes overall shape, arrangement of features and the way visual elements work together. An attractive design does not need to be highly decorated; simple designs can be effective when each feature appears deliberate and suits the object’s purpose.

aesthetic-design-and-evaluation.heading: Creating visual unity
aesthetic-design-and-evaluation.body: Visual balance is the way features appear evenly or deliberately arranged. Proportion describes size relationships between parts. Line can make a design look strong, calm, curved, sharp or flowing. Texture may come from the material or the way a surface is presented. Colour or finish can highlight grain, create contrast or produce a more unified appearance.

aesthetic-design-and-evaluation.heading: Evaluating the appearance
aesthetic-design-and-evaluation.body: An aesthetic evaluation should go beyond “I like it” or “it looks good”. Identify visible features and explain their effect. Balanced spacing may create order, while inconsistent shapes may distract from the overall design. Identify one realistic improvement, such as adjusting a proportion, simplifying a line or improving consistency.
